pointers.sentence: The docstring of `MigrationRecorder` names the difficulty: the table is itself used in creating models' tables, so it is the one thing that cannot be done through migrations (`django/db/migrations/recorder.py:MigrationRecorder`).

`MigrationRecorder.Migration` is a `classproperty`: its first read defines a model class and keeps it in `MigrationRecorder._migration_class`, and every later read returns the class kept (`django/db/migrations/recorder.py:MigrationRecorder.Migration`).

A model's class statement asks the main registry which application its module is in, and the registry refuses until the applications are loaded (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.get_containing_app_config`).

A model registers in the registry its options name ([The registry and its models](../startup/registry.md#registries-other-than-the-main-one)), so the main registry never has this one, and makemigrations, which reads the models off the main registry, makes no migration for it (`django/db/migrations/state.py:ProjectState.from_apps`).
A yes is thus remembered for the recorder's life, and a no is asked again each time (`django/db/migrations/recorder.py:MigrationRecorder.has_table`).

A `DatabaseError` from that is raised again as `MigrationSchemaMissing`, itself a `DatabaseError`, with the database's message in its own (`django/db/migrations/recorder.py:MigrationRecorder.ensure_schema`).

`ensure_schema` is the first thing `MigrationRecorder.record_applied` and `MigrationRecorder.record_unapplied` do, and `MigrationExecutor.migrate` calls it before carrying out a plan, unless the plan it is given is empty: its comment says the table must be there to record what is applied, but is not to be made when there is nothing to apply (`django/db/migrations/executor.py:MigrationExecutor.migrate`).

`MigrationRecorder.applied_migrations` returns a dictionary from each row's key to the row, an instance of the model; where there is no table it returns an empty one and makes none (`django/db/migrations/recorder.py:MigrationRecorder.applied_migrations`).

`MigrationExecutor.record_migration` writes the row of a key with `MigrationRecorder.record_applied`, or deletes it with `MigrationRecorder.record_unapplied` (`django/db/migrations/executor.py:MigrationExecutor.record_migration`).

The other caller of `record_unapplied` is migrate with `--prune`, for rows of the application it is given whose migrations are not on disk ([The migrate command, showmigrations and sqlmigrate](migrate.md)) (`django/core/management/commands/migrate.py:Command.handle`).

`MigrationLoader.check_consistent_history` reads the table for itself, on the connection it is given, to hold the rows against the graph ([Finding migrations: `MigrationLoader`](loader.md)). showmigrations reads it too, for its list (`django/core/management/commands/showmigrations.py:Command.show_list`).

A migration that replaces others (a squashed one) is the exception on both sides: `record_migration` first writes or deletes the rows of those it replaces, and `MigrationExecutor.check_replacements` writes that migration's own row, where it has none, once all it replaces is applied (`django/db/migrations/executor.py:MigrationExecutor.check_replacements`).

Django's readers use the keys of the dictionary `MigrationRecorder.applied_migrations` returns, and a row's time in one place: showmigrations, in its list, prints it from `--verbosity 2` up, but not for a migration that replaces others (`django/core/management/commands/showmigrations.py:Command.show_list`).
